cards.definition: To use something you already have to get an advantage.
cards.example:
- She leveraged her network to get the proposal in front of the CEO.
Ela alavancou a rede de contatos para levar a proposta até o CEO.
cards.note: Verbo e substantivo; no financeiro, alavancagem.

cards.definition: Agreement and support from the people who have to make it work.
cards.example:
- Without the team’s buy-in, even the best plan dies in a drawer.
Sem a adesão da equipe, até o melhor plano morre na gaveta.
cards.note: Get buy-in from — conquistar apoio antes de anunciar.

cards.definition: A reason someone gives for not agreeing.
cards.example:
- Good sellers welcome objections: each one is a map of the client’s mind.
Bons vendedores recebem bem as objeções: cada uma é um mapa da cabeça do cliente.

cards.definition: A situation where you accept something worse to get something better.
cards.example:
- Every decision is a trade-off between speed and quality.
Toda decisão é uma troca entre velocidade e qualidade.
cards.note: Não tem tradução exata — apresente como o preço de cada escolha.

cards.definition: A small push that changes what people choose.
cards.example:
- A small nudge, like a default option, changes what people choose.
Um empurrãozinho, como uma opção padrão, muda o que as pessoas escolhem.
cards.note: Termo da economia comportamental (Thaler); também verbo.

cards.definition: The quality of being believed and trusted.
cards.example:
- You build credibility with small promises delivered on time.
Você constrói credibilidade com promessas pequenas entregues no prazo.
cards.note: Build/lose credibility — constrói-se devagar, perde-se rápido.

cards.definition: An outcome where both sides gain something.
cards.example:
- Frame the deal as a win-win, or someone will feel like a loser.
Apresente o acordo como ganha-ganha, ou alguém vai se sentir perdedor.
cards.note: A win-win situation; o contrário é zero-sum (soma zero).

cards.definition: To imagine the situation from the other person's side.
cards.example:
- Before the pitch, put yourself in their shoes for five minutes.
Antes do pitch, coloque-se no lugar deles por cinco minutos.
cards.note: In someone’s shoes = na pele/situação de alguém.

cards.definition: A reason given to support an idea; also a heated disagreement.
cards.example:
- His argument was solid: data, a story, and a clear ask.
O argumento dele era sólido: dados, uma história e um pedido claro.
cards.note: We had an argument = nós brigamos (não “tivemos um argumento”).

cards.definition: Real, as opposed to what was assumed.
cards.example:
- The actual numbers tell a different story.
Os números reais contam uma história diferente.
cards.note: “Atual” = current: the current numbers = os números atuais.

questions.prompt: She _____ her network to get the proposal in front of the CEO.
questions.explanation: As a verb it takes the object directly — no “on”.
You GET or SECURE buy-in. It is uncountable — no “a buy-in”.
You RAISE an objection and then HANDLE it.

questions.prompt: Every decision is a _____ between speed and quality.
A small _____, like a default option, changes what people choose.
questions.explanation: “Nudge” is a gentle push, not a shove.
Credibility is BUILT slowly, LOST quickly.

questions.prompt: They keep the deadline and we keep the scope — it's a _____.
questions.explanation: Both sides gain; the hyphen stays.

questions.prompt: Before you answer the complaint, _____ for a minute.
questions.explanation: “In their shoes”, not “in their place” — the idiom is fixed.

questions.prompt: You give a reason to support your idea. You make an…
questions.explanation: “Argument” is both a reason and a row; context decides which.

options: The actual cost was double the estimate.
The actual manager started last year.
In the actual moment we are busy.
Actual prices are rising this year.
questions.answer: The actual cost was double the estimate.
